video_title: Larry McDonald: S&P 500 Could Crash 30% Over the Next Year
gist: Bear Traps Report founder Larry McDonald expects a ~30% S&P drop and a flat decade driven by AI concentration and the mega-IPO cash-out, while favoring beaten-down brands, discounted long bonds, hard-asset equities and stablecoin-linked plays amid financial repression.

insights.claim: The S&P 500 is about 50% tech, and Larry McDonald argues that any time one sector is this large of the market (as in 2000 and 2007) investors should run rather than walk.
insights.speaker: Larry McDonald
insights.so_what: Sector concentration is itself the risk signal; trim index exposure.
insights.quote: run don't walk the other way

insights.claim: SpaceX, Anthropic and OpenAI were worth about $360B three years ago and about $5.1T now; McDonald expects their entry into the Nasdaq 100 and eventually the S&P to be a massive cash-out by Silicon Valley billionaires onto passive and 401(k) investors.
insights.speaker: Larry McDonald
insights.so_what: Index inclusion of mega-IPOs creates forced passive demand at peak valuations; a supply-overhang risk.
insights.quote: This is the greatest cash out from billionaires in Silicon Valley we've ever seen.

insights.claim: McDonald predicts the S&P 500 drops 30% over the next year once the IPO dumping is absorbed, then stays flat for roughly eight years, as in 2000-2010.
insights.speaker: Larry McDonald
insights.so_what: Base case is a lost decade for index buy-and-hold, favoring selectivity.
insights.quote: the S&P is going to drop 30% over the next year

insights.claim: Nvidia and Apple together are about 13% of the S&P (Nvidia 8%, Apple 6%), versus the top two stocks being 5-6% in the 1990s and 2000s; McDonald says Nvidia will be cut in half over two to three years as older chips get cheaper.
insights.speaker: Larry McDonald
insights.so_what: Top-two concentration is at a record; Nvidia's pricing power is expected to erode with chip generations.

insights.claim: Around 60 'Hall of Fame' brands are down 35-80% while the index sits at all-time highs; sophisticated institutions are going long these brands and shorting the index or buying index puts into tax-loss season.
insights.speaker: Larry McDonald
insights.so_what: Long beaten-down quality brands versus short index is the pair being put on.

insights.claim: McDonald says the Nasdaq 100 market value rose from $12T in Q4 2022 to $30T in March to $43T now, versus under $1T in the metals ETF XME.
insights.speaker: Larry McDonald
insights.so_what: Wealth is hugely skewed to growth equities, so even small rotation into hard assets is large for that sector.

themes.theme: AI capex and Big Tech disruption

insights.claim: McDonald expects hyperscaler capex to slow within two to three months, driven by unclear payoff and political pushback, triggering a big reset in the Mag 7.
insights.speaker: Larry McDonald
insights.so_what: Capex deceleration is the catalyst to watch for AI-heavy indexes.
insights.quote: once these guys start to uh slow down the capex, which probably happens in the next two to three months

insights.claim: Meta is moving from $30-40B of free cash flow to roughly negative $20B, funding a free AI assistant with no barriers to entry that Google, Apple and others will also offer, making Meta a non-beneficiary.
insights.speaker: Larry McDonald
insights.so_what: Commoditized free AI products burn cash from monopoly businesses.

insights.claim: McDonald's three AI picks are Intuitive Surgical, Baxter and SLB, on the thesis that data ownership is the moat; he thinks SLB could double or triple in 5-10 years and robotic surgery share could rise manyfold.
insights.speaker: Larry McDonald
insights.so_what: AI winners are proprietary-data owners in the physical economy, not model sellers.

insights.claim: A bank-deposit AI agent could prompt savers to move zero-interest deposits to 4% alternatives; McDonald estimates $150B leaving Bank of America over one to five years, hitting a profit stream where the bank earns 4-5% on Treasuries while paying about 1%.
insights.speaker: Larry McDonald
insights.so_what: AI-driven deposit repricing is a second-order threat to bank net interest margin.

insights.claim: Long-dated bonds issued at 0-2% coupons during 2017-2021 (about $30T) are deeply discounted; an Apple 2.55% double-A bond trades at about 47 cents and could reach 72-73 if the 30-year returns to 4%, roughly 18% a year over three years.
insights.speaker: Larry McDonald
insights.so_what: Discount long bonds offer equity-like returns with rate-decline optionality.
insights.quote: bonds are starting to offer equity like returns because they've crashed like it's 1929

insights.claim: Institutions are pairing deeply discounted Apple bonds with two-year puts on Apple equity: a rate rise that hurts the bond would also hurt consumer-facing Apple stock, making the hedge a seesaw.
insights.speaker: Larry McDonald
insights.so_what: Cross-asset hedging of bond duration with equity puts exploits mismatched volatility.

insights.claim: McDonald sees US 10- and 30-year yields possibly going higher in a final blowoff, then reversing, and sees a bear-market rally in TLT worth 10-20-30% including coupons into next year.
insights.speaker: Larry McDonald
insights.so_what: Rate spike likely marks a duration buying point.

insights.claim: A debt-ceiling hit in January with split Congress could leave the Treasury with about $1T in the TGA plus $300B of extraordinary measures, meaning possibly no net Treasury issuance from roughly March to July next year, supportive for bond prices.
insights.speaker: Larry McDonald
insights.so_what: Supply pause is a mechanical tailwind for bonds in the first half of next year.

insights.claim: Rising oil and rates (12-month Treasury up 100bp, distillates up 60-120%) have delivered a roughly $300B hit to the US consumer, which McDonald cites as the reason McDonald's and Home Depot are down 30-35%.
insights.speaker: Larry McDonald
insights.so_what: Consumer stress is already priced in many brands; the supernova-economy analogy implies a slowdown.

insights.claim: Nike is 75-80% off highs with about $3B free cash flow and a $51B market cap; McDonald calls the volume capitulation category 5 and 30% below the 200-month moving average, a buy ahead of the 2028 Olympics.
insights.speaker: Larry McDonald
insights.so_what: Capitulation volume in a major brand is his model for a contrarian long.
insights.quote: You do that every day of the week and twice on Sunday.

themes.theme: Hard assets, inflation and financial repression

insights.claim: Using the 1968-81 analogy, McDonald says industrials, materials and energy were 50% of the S&P by 1981 versus about 14% today, and expects trillions to rotate into hard-asset companies, taking the weight to 20-30% over five years.
insights.speaker: Larry McDonald
insights.so_what: A sustained inflation regime favors asset-owning companies over software and long-duration growth.

insights.claim: In a 3-6% inflation regime, discounted-cash-flow models value a software company's distant cash flows much less, while owners of oil, gas and metals see asset values rise.
insights.speaker: Larry McDonald
insights.so_what: Duration of cash flows determines relative equity performance in inflation.

insights.claim: AI buildout is inflationary at first (Caterpillar up 300% in about 18 months, copper for power grids), and even if AI slows, rebalancing from a tiny household commodity allocation (about 1% versus 4% in 1981) supports hard-asset equities; natural gas names like Antero and Range offer 8-10% free cash flow yields with 10-15% buybacks.
insights.speaker: Larry McDonald
insights.so_what: Hard-asset equities have valuation and allocation support independent of AI demand.

insights.claim: McDonald says the US faces a $40T debt hole with only default or inflation as exits, expects Fed-Treasury coordination and financial repression like post-WWII, and cites US fiscal and monetary response since COVID of about $17T versus $4T after Lehman.
insights.speaker: Larry McDonald
insights.so_what: Policy suppression of real rates pushes capital into hard assets.
insights.quote: when you run 6% deficits, the fiscal and monetary response this time since co is 17 trillion

insights.claim: McDonald thinks Washington's sanctions and asset seizures triggered central banks to sell Treasuries for gold, citing China's Treasury holdings down about $600-700B, and speculates the US could revalue its gold or use it as collateral.
insights.speaker: Larry McDonald
insights.so_what: Reserve diversification into gold is structural; a gold revaluation is a possible policy tool.

insights.claim: Stablecoins have grown from about $100B to $300-350B and McDonald expects $1-1.5T in five years, with issuers holding mostly T-bills, creating front-end Treasury demand that functions like soft yield-curve control.
insights.speaker: Larry McDonald
insights.so_what: Stablecoin growth is a largely unpriced Treasury bill buyer, helping finance US debt.
insights.quote: What's not priced in is the awareness of stable coins.

insights.claim: McDonald highlights Circle (up from 62 to the 90s this year) as the main investable stablecoin trade, contingent on the Clarity Act, with Tether and Circle at 60-80% market share.
insights.speaker: Larry McDonald
insights.so_what: Few listed vehicles exist; Circle is the proxy.

insights.claim: McDonald's firm bought Bitcoin on the summer lows and recently lightened it, citing quantum computing: he says about 50% of institutional investors now see it as a threat in five to seven years.
insights.speaker: Larry McDonald
insights.so_what: Quantum risk is moving from joke to consensus concern and favors cybersecurity baskets on dips.
